item.title: Privacy Policy
item.content:encoded:
Last updated: 12 May 2026. Version 1.0.

This Privacy Policy explains how Booming Venture handles personal data. We follow the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Dutch implementation (Uitvoeringswet AVG), and the ePrivacy obligations in the Dutch Telecommunicatiewet. If anything below is unclear, email info@boomingventure.com and we will rewrite it.

1. Who we are

Booming Venture is the data controller for personal data collected through this website.

  • Address: Breedveldsingel 1, 3055 PG Rotterdam, The Netherlands
  • Email: info@boomingventure.com
  • KvK (Chamber of Commerce): 96442018
  • VAT (BTW): NL005211648B76

We have not appointed a Data Protection Officer. Our processing does not meet the thresholds in GDPR Article 37(1), but you can reach our privacy contact at the email above.

2. What personal data we collect

  • Identification and contact data you give us: name, work email, company, role, phone (optional).
  • Communication content: the message you send via the contact form, support emails, chatbot transcripts.
  • Billing data for clients: invoicing details and VAT identifiers.
  • Website usage data: IP address, browser, device, pages viewed, referrer, time on page. Most of this is collected by Google Analytics in pseudonymous form.
  • Marketing data for clients: campaign performance numbers on platforms we manage for you. This is processed under a separate Data Processing Agreement.
  • Lead-magnet data: the email you enter to download the Growth Guide or UNIFY Framework guide, plus the source field.

3. Why we process it and the legal basis

  • To deliver the services you hire us for. Legal basis: performance of a contract (Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR).
  • To respond to your enquiry and follow up. Legal basis: legitimate interest in answering people who contact us (Art. 6(1)(f)). You can object at any time.
  • To send marketing emails to subscribers and existing clients. Legal basis: consent for new subscribers (Art. 6(1)(a) plus Telecommunicatiewet art. 11.7), or the soft opt-in for existing clients who can unsubscribe from every email.
  • To improve the website and security. Legal basis: legitimate interest (Art. 6(1)(f)), with a balancing test on record.
  • To comply with tax law. Legal basis: legal obligation, seven-year retention under Algemene wet inzake rijksbelastingen art. 52.

4. Cookies and similar trackers

Cookies that are strictly necessary for the site to work (session, security, load balancing) run by default. Every other cookie, including analytics, marketing pixels, and the DataSpeak chat, only loads after you accept it through the consent banner. You can change or withdraw consent any time via the cookie button in the footer.

The categories we use:

  • Strictly necessary: WordPress session, cookie-consent record, Cloudflare bot mitigation.
  • Analytics: Google Analytics 4 via Google Tag Manager. Pseudonymous user ID, page views, events. 14-month retention.
  • Marketing: Brevo tracking pixel for email engagement on opt-in lists.
  • Functional: DataSpeak conversational AI cookies when the chatbot is opened.

5. Who we share data with

We use the following processors. Each has a Data Processing Agreement with us under GDPR Article 28.

  • Brevo (Sendinblue SAS, France) for transactional and marketing email.
  • DataSpeak B.V. (Netherlands) for the website chatbot.
  • Google Ireland Ltd for Google Analytics and Google Tag Manager. Data flows to Google LLC in the United States.
  • Cloudflare Inc. for content delivery and security.
  • Our WordPress hosting provider.

We do not sell personal data and we do not share it for cross-context behavioural advertising.

6. Transfers outside the EU/EEA

Google and Cloudflare process data in the United States. Both companies are certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (Commission adequacy decision of 10 July 2023). As a fallback we rely on Standard Contractual Clauses (Commission Decision 2021/914) and we have transfer impact assessments on file. You can request a copy by emailing us.

7. How long we keep data

  • Client engagement records and invoicing: 7 years after the contract ends (tax obligation).
  • Prospect and lead data: 24 months from the last interaction.
  • Newsletter subscribers: until unsubscribe plus 30 days of suppression-list retention.
  • Chatbot transcripts: 12 months.
  • Google Analytics: 14 months (default).
  • Server logs: 14 days for security forensics.

8. Your rights

Under GDPR you can:

  • Request a copy of the personal data we hold (right of access, Art. 15).
  • Correct inaccurate data (Art. 16).
  • Ask us to delete data when there is no longer a legal reason to keep it (Art. 17).
  • Ask us to restrict processing while a dispute is resolved (Art. 18).
  • Receive your data in a portable format (Art. 20).
  • Object to processing based on legitimate interest (Art. 21).
  • Withdraw consent at any time without losing the lawfulness of past processing (Art. 7(3)).

Email info@boomingventure.com to use any of these rights. We respond within one month (Art. 12(3)). You also have the right to file a complaint with the Dutch supervisory authority, Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens.

9. Automated decisions and AI tools

The Funnel Leak Calculator and ROI Forecaster on this site produce estimates based on the numbers you type in. They do not store your inputs, do not profile you, and do not make any decision that has a legal or similarly significant effect on you. The DataSpeak chatbot is an AI system, and you will see a disclosure that you are chatting with one before the conversation starts.

For client work, any automated profiling we run on a campaign is governed by the Data Processing Agreement with that client.

10. Security

The site uses TLS in transit. Access to admin systems is restricted and logged. Passwords are hashed. Backups are encrypted. We test our defences regularly.

11. Data breaches

If a breach poses a risk to your rights, we notify the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens within 72 hours under Art. 33 GDPR. If the risk is high, we notify you directly under Art. 34.

12. Children

Our services are aimed at businesses. We do not knowingly collect data from anyone under 16.

13. Changes to this policy

We update this page when our processing changes or when the law does. The version date at the top tells you when. For material changes that affect existing subscribers, we send an email.

item.title: Terms of Service
item.content:encoded:
Last updated: 12 May 2026. Version 1.0. Governed by Dutch law.

These Terms apply to every quote, agreement, and engagement between Booming Venture and a client. By signing a Statement of Work or paying an invoice, the client accepts these Terms. The Dutch version controls in case of translation conflict.

1. Parties and contact

"We", "us", or "Booming Venture" means Booming Venture, registered at Breedveldsingel 1, 3055 PG Rotterdam, the Netherlands, KvK 96442018, VAT NL005211648B76. "Client" means the natural or legal person who engages us. "Services" means the work described in the Statement of Work (SOW) or proposal we agree on.

2. Scope of services

We deliver what the SOW says we deliver, on the timeline it sets. Anything outside that scope is a change request. Change requests need written approval (email counts) and adjust fees and timing.

3. Best-efforts obligation, not result

This is an overeenkomst van opdracht under Article 7:400 of the Dutch Civil Code: a best-efforts obligation, not a result-based one. We commit to using our skill and experience, applying current best practice, and acting in the client's interest. We do not, and cannot, guarantee specific outcomes such as search rankings, leads generated, conversion rates, return on ad spend, or revenue. Marketing and AI performance depend on platforms, market conditions, the client's product, brand, pricing, sales follow-up, and many factors outside our control.

4. Fees, invoicing, and late payment

  • Retainers are invoiced monthly in advance. Project fees follow the schedule in the SOW.
  • Payment is due within 14 days of the invoice date unless agreed otherwise.
  • For overdue B2B invoices we charge the statutory commercial interest rate (wettelijke handelsrente, Art. 6:119a Dutch Civil Code) plus extrajudicial collection costs (Besluit vergoeding voor buitengerechtelijke incassokosten).
  • We may suspend services on non-payment (Art. 6:262 Dutch Civil Code) after one written reminder.
  • All fees exclude VAT. VAT is added at the applicable rate.

5. Term and termination

  • The initial term is set in the SOW. After it, the agreement continues month to month unless terminated.
  • Either party can end the agreement with one full calendar month notice in writing.
  • If the client terminates an active engagement early, a kill-fee equal to the remaining retainer in the current term, or 50% thereof if the SOW says so, becomes due.
  • Either party can terminate immediately if the other commits a material breach that is not cured within 14 days of written notice, or in case of bankruptcy or insolvency proceedings.
  • On termination, the client pays for work delivered up to the effective date. Sections that by nature should survive (IP, confidentiality, liability, governing law) do.

6. Intellectual property

  • On full payment, the client owns the final deliverables created for the client and may use them without restriction.
  • Our pre-existing frameworks, methodologies, templates, prompt libraries, internal tools, and the UNIFY Framework™ remain our property. The client gets a perpetual, non-exclusive licence to use them as part of the delivered work.
  • The client grants us a non-exclusive, royalty-free licence to use deliverables and the client's name and logo in our portfolio, case studies, and marketing, unless the client opts out in writing.
  • Third-party assets (stock images, licensed fonts, paid plugins) follow their own licence terms, passed through to the client.

7. Confidentiality

Both parties keep confidential information confidential for three years after the engagement ends. Standard carve-outs apply: information that is public, already known to the receiving party, independently developed, or required to be disclosed by law or regulator.

8. Data protection

Where we process personal data on the client's behalf, the client is the controller and we are the processor under GDPR Article 28. A Data Processing Agreement is annexed to the SOW and prevails over these Terms for data-protection matters. The client warrants that it has a valid legal basis for any personal data it provides to us, including customer lists and CRM exports, and indemnifies us against any third-party claim that arises from a failure to do so.

9. Liability

  • Our total liability under or in connection with the agreement, in any 12-month period, is capped at the fees the client paid us in that period.
  • If a claim arises in the first three months of the engagement, the cap is one month of retainer.
  • We are not liable for indirect or consequential damages, lost profits, lost revenue, loss of data, loss of goodwill, or reputational harm.
  • The cap and exclusions do not apply to liability that cannot be limited under Dutch law, such as intent or gross negligence (per Art. 6:248 Dutch Civil Code).

10. Platform and third-party dependencies

Our work depends on third-party platforms (Google, Meta, LinkedIn, TikTok, HubSpot, Brevo, OpenAI, Anthropic, and others). We are not responsible for changes in their algorithms, pricing, policies, API behaviour, account suspensions, or service availability. If a platform change degrades or breaks part of the work, we will redesign in good faith within the existing scope where possible.

11. Force majeure

Neither party is liable for failure to perform due to events beyond reasonable control (Art. 6:75 Dutch Civil Code), including but not limited to natural disaster, war, terrorism, civil unrest, strike, public health emergency, regulator action, internet outages affecting the country, and major outages of third-party platforms we depend on. If the event lasts more than 60 days, either party can terminate without penalty for work not yet delivered.

12. Client obligations and deemed approval

  • The client provides accurate, complete, and timely information, access, and approvals needed for us to deliver.
  • The client names a single decision-maker for the engagement.
  • Any deliverable shared with the client is considered approved if the client does not raise specific written objections within five working days. Approved deliverables can still be revised under change control.
  • The client warrants that any content, brand asset, product claim, or audience list it provides does not infringe third-party rights and complies with applicable advertising rules. The client indemnifies us against claims that arise from it.

13. Subcontracting and assignment

We may engage subcontractors. We remain responsible for their work. The client cannot assign the agreement to a third party without our written consent, which we will not unreasonably withhold.

14. Governing law and dispute resolution

Dutch law governs the agreement, with the UN Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods excluded. Before starting litigation, parties try to resolve disputes in good faith and, if helpful, through a mediator. Otherwise the Rechtbank Rotterdam has exclusive jurisdiction.

15. Miscellaneous

  • If any provision is unenforceable, the rest stays in force and parties replace it with one that comes closest to its commercial intent.
  • Amendments need to be in writing and signed by both parties.
  • These Terms together with the SOW and any annexes are the entire agreement. They prevail over the client's purchase conditions (Art. 6:225(3) Dutch Civil Code battle-of-forms).
  • No waiver of any breach counts as a waiver of any later breach.

item.title: Disclaimer
item.content:encoded:
Last updated: 12 May 2026.

The information on this website, including all articles, calculators, chatbot responses, and guides, is provided for general information only. Read this page before relying on anything you find here.

No professional advice

Content on this site is not a substitute for professional advice. The Funnel Leak Calculator and ROI Forecaster produce illustrative estimates based on numbers you enter and standard assumptions. Their outputs are not financial advice, legal advice, tax advice, or accounting advice, and they are not promises about future business results. Make important decisions with a qualified adviser who knows your business.

AI-generated content and EU AI Act transparency

Some content and tools on this site involve artificial intelligence:

  • The chatbot in the bottom-right corner is an AI system. Replies are machine-generated. Verify anything important before acting on it.
  • The Funnel Leak Calculator and ROI Forecaster produce automated estimates. They do not profile you, do not store inputs, and do not make any decision that has a legal or similarly significant effect on you.
  • Articles on this blog are written and edited by humans. Where any AI assistance is used (for example research summarising), the published version is reviewed by a human author.

We disclose these under Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the EU AI Act). If you have questions about how an AI feature works, email info@boomingventure.com.

Accuracy of content

We try to keep articles current and accurate, but the world changes faster than our editorial calendar. Strategies, platform features, prices, and regulations cited in blog posts may be outdated by the time you read them. We do not warrant that the content is complete, accurate, or fit for any specific purpose.

Third-party links and tools

This site links to third-party websites, products, and services. Including a link is not an endorsement. We are not responsible for the content, accuracy, privacy practices, or service availability of any third party.

Results, case studies, and testimonials

Numbers and quotes from clients are real, but they describe specific situations. Past results are not a guarantee of future performance. Your results depend on your product, market, team, and execution.

Forward-looking statements

Forecasts, predictions, and projections published anywhere on this site, including in the ROI Forecaster, involve assumptions and uncertainty. Treat them as scenarios, not as facts.

Trademarks

UNIFY Framework™ is a trademark of Booming Venture. Other product names, logos, and trademarks belong to their respective owners and are used for identification only.

Contact

For questions about this disclaimer, email info@boomingventure.com.

item.title: What is AI marketing? (And why it’s not just hype)
item.excerpt:encoded: AI marketing isn’t just a buzzword, it’s a fundamental shift in how we understand and engage customers. Discover the data-driven strategies that are transforming business growth.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

AI marketing is the systematic use of machine learning, generative models, and predictive analytics inside marketing decisions and content. According to the McKinsey 2025 State of AI report, 78% of organisations now use AI in at least one business function, up from 55% in 2023. Done well, it changes how you target, write, score, and report. Done badly, it gives you faster spam.

AI marketing has moved from buzzword to operating model in roughly three years. The HubSpot State of Marketing survey of more than 1,200 marketers found that AI-using teams report 30% higher productivity on average. The question for 2026 is no longer whether to adopt it, but where it actually moves the metric.

What is AI marketing?

AI marketing is the systematic use of machine learning, generative models, and predictive analytics across the customer journey to make targeting, content, and decisioning faster and more personal.

The systematic part matters. One ChatGPT prompt does not make a marketing program AI-driven. A workflow that scores leads, drafts variations, A/B tests them, and feeds the result back into the model does. The shift is structural, not tactical. Five years ago, a CRM segmentation was a SQL query a marketer wrote on Monday and forgot by Friday. Today the same segmentation updates itself every time someone opens an email or stalls in checkout. The marketer's job moved from authoring rules to designing the loop.

Why did AI marketing take off now?

AI marketing scaled in 2024 to 2025 because three changes converged: cheaper inference, mature first-party data systems, and the end of last-click attribution.

Running a useful language model on a single email cost ten cents in 2022. It is closer to a tenth of that now, according to benchmarks tracked by Artificial Analysis. That makes per-customer personalisation a budget line, not a science project. The death of third-party cookies forced brands to invest in a first-party data layer, which gives AI something to chew on. And marketing-mix modelling and incrementality testing replaced last-click in most credible teams. AI loves a stable training signal, and revenue is one.

What counts as AI marketing and what does not?

Real AI marketing learns from outcomes. Anything that surfaces a static prediction or a one-shot rewrite without a feedback loop is automation with marketing on the label.

Counts: predictive lead scoring trained on closed-won data, generative subject-line testing where winners feed the model, RFM models that update weekly, dynamic landing pages that select hero copy by visitor intent, look-alike audiences built from highest-LTV cohorts, conversational chat using live product data.

Does not count: a static "AI rewrite this paragraph" button, email send-time optimisation based on a single rule, vendor demos where the AI feature is a dashboard label.

Where does AI marketing actually move the number?

Four areas show consistent payback: predictive lead scoring (15 to 30 percent SQL-to-customer lift), generative ad creative at scale, behaviour-driven lifecycle email, and AI-summarised reporting.

  1. Lead scoring. Replacing manual scoring with a model trained on your own closed-won and closed-lost data lifts SQL-to-customer conversion 15 to 30 percent. Humans build rules around the leads they remember; models look at all of them.
  2. Content variation at scale. If you run paid search or paid social with more than 50 ad groups, AI-generated copy variations beat static creative within two to three weeks. The trick is the workflow that promotes winners and kills losers automatically.
  3. Email and lifecycle. Subject-line testing, send-time optimisation, and behaviour-triggered sequences all benefit. Revenue per email rises 15 to 35 percent when product recommendations are individually personalised (Klaviyo benchmarks).
  4. Reporting and decisioning. Models that watch your data daily and surface anomalies, drops, and opportunities save a senior analyst's week, every week.

How should I start without burning a year?

Start with one decision made often and badly. Get the data right before the model. Set up the feedback loop. Most teams who fail skip the data step and ship a demo instead of a program.

  1. Pick one decision. Lead scoring is the usual answer for B2B; product recommendations on the cart page for B2C.
  2. Clean the data first. AI fails for the same reason BI fails: dirty inputs. Spend the first month on the data layer.
  3. Set up the loop. Outputs, outcomes, feedback. If you cannot trace from a model decision to a revenue change, you have a demo, not a program.

Use the Funnel Leak Calculator to see which stage is leaking most revenue, then point the first AI project at that stage.

Frequently asked questions

Is AI marketing different from marketing automation?

Yes. Automation runs predefined rules. AI marketing chooses what to do based on signals the rules did not anticipate.

Do I need a data scientist?

Not for the starter wins. HubSpot AI, Klaviyo predictive analytics, and Customer.io's AI features ship usable models out of the box. You need a data scientist when you start training on your own data, usually in year two.

What does AI marketing cost?

Licence cost is the small line. The work to clean data, design loops, and edit AI output is the real budget. Plan for a 70/30 split between people and software.

What about the EU AI Act?

Most marketing AI is "limited risk" under Article 50 of Regulation 2024/1689. You disclose that users are interacting with an AI system (chatbots) and mark AI-generated content. Transparency obligations apply from August 2026.

How fast do results show?

Lead scoring: 4 to 6 weeks. Lifecycle email: 30 days. Predictive media buying: 60 days. Full attribution rebuild: 6 to 12 months.

AI marketing is not a category of tools. It is an operating model where decisions get faster and more personal because a learning system sits inside the workflow. Start with the worst leak in your funnel. Pick one model. Build the loop. Then expand. See how we structure this work across the UNIFY Framework.

item.title: 7 biggest growth mistakes premium brands make
item.excerpt:encoded: Premium brands often fall into growth traps that commoditize their positioning. Learn the 7 critical mistakes and how to avoid them while scaling sustainably.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Premium brands lose more growth to commodity reflexes than to competitors. The seven repeating mistakes: discount habit, volume chasing, positioning drift, wrong channels, lazy creative, weak retention, and vibes-based measurement. According to Bain's 2024 luxury study, the brands defending margin in soft markets all share two traits: pricing discipline and audited retention.

Premium has a margin problem only when growth gets sloppy. The brands that scale without losing pricing power keep doing the boring work: protecting position, choosing fewer customers better, and refusing the shortcuts that look like growth on a dashboard. Across more than 30 premium brand audits we have run at Booming Venture, the same seven mistakes show up, ranked here by how often they bite. Ehrenberg-Bass Institute research backs the strategic framing: penetration drives growth, but only inside the right buyer set.

Why does the discounting reflex hurt premium brands so badly?

The discounting reflex resets the anchor price in the buyer's mind. The cost is not the single discount, it is every future full-price sale that now feels expensive by comparison.

Customers who bought at 30 percent off treat the discounted price as the real one and wait for the next sale. Harvard Business Review documented this as far back as 2010, and the pattern repeats in every category we audit. If you must discount, do it under a different brand name, on a private list, with a time-bound mechanism. Better: bundle, upgrade, or add a limited service tier instead of cutting price.

How does chasing volume break premium positioning?

Premium positioning assumes scarcity. Optimising for monthly orders pulls in the wrong audience, dilutes brand cues, and floods downstream systems with low-LTV buyers.

Paid traffic gets cheaper but it brings the wrong audience. Influencers get bigger but they sit further from the buyer. Email lists grow but open rates fall. Track quality of growth alongside volume. A useful metric is the ratio of new customer LTV to acquired CAC at the cohort level. If new cohorts are cheaper to acquire but worth less, you have growth on paper and decline in reality.

What is positioning drift and how do you catch it?

Positioning drift is the quiet quarterly rewriting of the brand by every new marketer who joins. After three years the brand sounds like every competitor. Test new copy against a fixed one-sentence anchor to catch it.

Founders ship a brand. The team grows. New marketers join. They each rewrite the homepage a little. The fix is a brand book that is short, opinionated, and used. Twelve pages beats sixty. Include the one sentence that explains why anyone should pay 2x. Test every piece of new copy against it.

Which other mistakes round out the seven?

Four more: wrong channel mix copied from mass-market playbooks, lazy creative outsourced to the cheapest bid, no retention machine, and measurement that is vibes-based on brand and last-click on performance.

  1. Wrong channel mix. Premium B2B buyers live on LinkedIn, podcasts, and trade publications. Premium consumers come from PR, peer referral, and high-intent search. Spend follows attention.
  2. Lazy creative. Ship 3 to 5 new variations weekly, brand as constant, message as variable. Reject anything that could have been written for a competitor.
  3. No retention machine. Premium customers churn quietly. Build a retention loop with a named owner, a 30-60-90 day post-purchase sequence, and a quarterly check-in for top-tier accounts.
  4. Vibes-based measurement. Without a basic marketing-mix model or incrementality framework, every channel argues for more budget and no channel can prove it. Start with a 30-day geographic holdout on the largest paid channel.

Use the Funnel Leak Calculator to size the cost of your current retention rate before you decide where to invest the first 90 days.

Frequently asked questions

How long does it take to fix these?

Positioning and creative shift in a quarter. Retention and measurement take 6 to 12 months because they touch culture, not just process.

Which mistake matters most?

For most premium brands we audit, retention is the largest unfixed problem. It compounds faster than any acquisition channel.

Should premium brands run paid ads at all?

Yes, but with tight intent matching. Branded search and high-intent retargeting beat broad prospecting nine times out of ten in this segment.

Is Black Friday off the table for premium brands?

Not always. But the version that protects margin uses scarcity and bundles, not stacked percentage discounts, and is run once a year, not monthly.

What does a brand book actually contain?

Audience definition, one-sentence value proposition, three claim pillars with proof, banned phrases, approved tone, and 6 to 12 fully-written example posts.

Pick two mistakes from this list. Fix them in 90 days. Ignore the other five until you have. Most growth-stage premium brands try to fix everything at once and end up moving none of them. Our Strategic Consulting engagement exists specifically to sequence the work.

item.title: Why traditional marketing strategies fail in 2025
item.excerpt:encoded: The marketing playbook from 2020 is obsolete. Consumer behavior, technology, and market dynamics have fundamentally shifted. Here’s what works now.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

The 2020 marketing playbook broke because three things changed at once: third-party tracking died, AI Overviews ate the top of search, and buyers compressed their own funnels. According to SparkToro's zero-click study, 58.5% of US Google searches now end without a click, rising to 83% when AI Overviews are present. The fix is first-party data, signal-based selling, and brand investment that earns the shortlist.

Marketing teams that ran the 2020 playbook in 2025 quietly underperformed for two years. The pipeline still showed leads. The dashboard still showed conversions. The number that mattered, revenue per dollar of marketing spend, fell. Gartner's 2024 CMO Spend Survey found marketing budgets shrank to 7.7% of revenue, the lowest since 2014. Here is why, and what to do instead.

Which three changes broke the old playbook?

Third-party tracking died after Apple's ATT, AI Overviews compressed top-of-funnel search, and B2B buyers now complete 60 to 80% of the journey before they speak to anyone.

Apple's ATT prompt, Safari's tracking defaults, and Chrome's gradual cookie removal eliminated the targeting precision that made 2018 to 2021 performance marketing work. Look-alike audiences degraded. Retargeting reach collapsed on iOS. CPMs rose. Then Google's AI Overviews compressed informational queries into a single answer box. Ahrefs analysis shows informational click-through dropped 30 to 60% on queries where Overviews appear. And Gartner B2B Buyer survey confirms modern buyers complete most evaluation before contacting sales.

What still works in 2025 and beyond?

Three things produce predictable results: brand investment that drives branded search, first-party customer data systems, and trust signals at high-intent decision moments.

  • Brand at the top. Branded search volume is the most reliable forward indicator of pipeline. Invest in being the brand people search for, not just the one Google decides to serve.
  • First-party data systems. A customer data platform tied to email and CRM gives you the targeting precision that third-party cookies used to provide.
  • Trust signals at high-intent moments. Case studies, named customer logos, peer reviews, and security pages convert in 2025 because trust is what is rare.

What has stopped working?

Three patterns have failed: last-click attribution that systematically over-credits paid search, long nurture emails to cold lists, and generic gated content that buyers can ChatGPT in two minutes.

  • Last-click attribution. Use marketing-mix modelling or incrementality testing. Last-click over-credits paid search and underfunds brand and PR by up to 80% according to mid-2025 MMM rebuilds.
  • Long nurture emails to cold lists. Engagement died after 2022. Cold acquisition email works only with sender warming, segmentation, and short copy.
  • Generic gated content. If the ebook says what every ebook says, gating costs you the signal it provides. Make it specific or make it free.

What should you build instead?

A three-layer stack: a demand layer above the funnel, a signal layer that catches in-market accounts, and an automation layer tying lifecycle behaviour to communication.

  1. Demand layer. Podcast, LinkedIn presence from named people, ungated content. Measured by branded search lift and direct traffic.
  2. Signal layer. Track when accounts view pricing, return to the site, or hit comparison pages. Pass those signals to sales the same day.
  3. Automation layer. Lifecycle email tied to behaviour. AI-driven scoring and routing. Quarterly model retraining.

This stack is harder to set up than the 2020 funnel, and once it works it is more durable. We implement it in 90-day phases through the UNIFY Framework.

Frequently asked questions

How long until results show from the new playbook?

Brand and demand: 2 to 4 quarters in pipeline. Signal-based selling: 30 to 60 days, because you are reallocating effort, not building new audiences.

Do I need to fire my paid agency?

Probably not. Most agencies can run signal-based playbooks if you give them the signals. The question is whether they still report last-click on the dashboard. If yes, change the dashboard.

Is SEO dead?

No. Middle and bottom of funnel grow on search even as informational top-of-funnel shrinks. Optimise for comparison, alternative, and pricing queries.

What about generative engine optimisation?

GEO is real. Front-load answer capsules in the first 30% of articles. Add FAQPage schema. Ship llms.txt. Princeton's GEO paper documents the tactics that raise AI-citation likelihood.

How much budget moves from one layer to another?

Most teams find a 30/40/30 split (demand/signal/automation) works better than the legacy 70% on bottom-of-funnel paid.

The new playbook is less linear than the old one. It works because buyers stopped being linear. Run the ROI Forecaster against your current and proposed channel mix to see the cost-of-acquisition shift before you commit.

item.title: How AI automation strengthens (not replaces) your marketing team
item.excerpt:encoded: AI isn’t here to replace marketers, it’s here to amplify their capabilities. Discover how smart automation can free your team to focus on strategy and creativity.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

AI does not replace marketers, it absorbs the work marketers should never have been doing. According to the McKinsey State of AI survey, marketing and sales teams using generative AI report a 30% productivity lift on average. The composition of the work changes; headcount does not. Strategy stays human.

Every marketing leader gets the same question from the CMO right now: how is AI changing your team's headcount plan? The honest answer is that AI is changing what the team does, not how many people you need. The work AI absorbs and the work it does not are now both clearly defined. HubSpot's State of Marketing puts marketing-team AI adoption at 71% in 2024 to 2025.

What kind of marketing work does AI absorb best?

AI absorbs three categories cleanly: variant production at scale, translation and localisation, and data summarisation. Each cuts senior-marketer time without measurable quality loss.

  • Variant production. Twenty ad headlines, ten email subject lines, twelve image prompts. AI is faster than any human at producing the long tail of variants that performance marketing eats.
  • Translation and localisation. First-pass translation across five EU languages, then native edit. Cost falls 60 to 80%. Quality holds if the editor is a native speaker.
  • Data summarisation. Weekly dashboard read-outs, anomaly callouts, account-level briefings before sales calls. Marketers spend less time pasting numbers into Slack.

What work does AI still not absorb in 2026?

The strategic layer stays human: brand voice, original research, customer relationships, editorial judgement, and negotiation with platforms and stakeholders.

If your job is one of these, AI makes you better. If your job is mostly variant production, the job description changes. Andrew Chen at a16z has written about the same pattern across product and growth: the high end gets more valuable, the low end gets cheaper, the middle gets squeezed.

How does team composition shift over three years?

Three years from now, healthy mid-market marketing teams will have fewer pure execution roles, more analysts, the same number of writers, and one dedicated AI lead.

  • Fewer pure execution roles. The junior who wrote 20 versions of the same ad becomes a strategist editing AI outputs.
  • More analysts. Someone designs the feedback loops, measures what works, retrains the models.
  • Same number of writers. The good ones publish more. The mediocre ones get replaced by AI plus a senior editor.
  • One AI lead. Either a hire or a third of a senior marketer's time. Owns the AI roadmap, the tool stack, and the prompt library.

How should you introduce AI without breaking team culture?

Run AI side by side with the team for one quarter, share the output data publicly, pay for senior editing rather than skimping on it, and publish your AI use policy before customers ask.

  1. Start with a single workflow. Lead scoring, subject-line testing, or content briefs. One win before broadening.
  2. Run AI side by side with the team. Compare output for a quarter. Trust grows from seeing the work, not from a town-hall slide.
  3. Pay for senior, save on junior. The mistake we see most often is shipping AI output without senior editing. Quality drops fast.
  4. Publish your AI use policy. Be explicit with team and customers about what gets AI assistance. The EU AI Act Article 50 requires some of this in 2026 anyway.

A B2B SaaS team of seven we work with shifted from 70% execution / 30% strategy to roughly 40% execution / 60% strategy in 2024. Headcount stayed the same. Published content volume tripled. Pipeline grew 38%. The two changes that mattered most were a custom GPT for content briefs and a Klaviyo lifecycle setup tied to product usage signals.

Frequently asked questions

Will junior marketers still get hired?

Yes, but the role looks different. Less hand production, more output editing, more analytical work. The strongest juniors learn to direct AI rather than compete with it.

How do I know if my AI use is degrading content quality?

Measure engagement at the cohort level. If AI-assisted content has lower scroll depth and reply rate than the human-only baseline, the editing is too thin.

What is the right budget split for AI tools?

Mid-market 2025 to 2026: 8 to 15% of marketing tools budget. Skewed toward Copilot or Gemini for the team plus one or two specialised tools for content or analysis.

How do customers feel about AI-assisted content?

Survey data is mixed. The pragmatic stance: disclose substantial AI authorship, do not disclose AI-assisted research, and stay accountable for accuracy in either case.

Will my CMO want to cut headcount?

Some will try. The teams that come out ahead reinvest the time saved into higher-impact work rather than running the same playbook with fewer people.

Teams that thrive in this transition treat AI as a senior intern, not a replacement. Give it the right work, edit its output, measure the difference, and free your humans to do the things that compound. Our AI-Powered Solutions engagement sequences this transition.

item.title: The future of content: AI as your creative assistant
item.excerpt:encoded: Content creation is evolving beyond human vs. AI to human + AI collaboration.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

The argument about AI versus human content is over. The teams that win treat AI as a creative assistant that compresses the boring parts. Gartner's 2025 marketing predictions expect 30% of all outbound marketing messages from large organisations to be synthetically generated by 2026. The output that ranks and converts is human voice plus AI speed.

Two years ago marketers asked whether AI could write their content. Today the question is what jobs AI does best inside a content workflow that still has humans at the top and bottom. Here is the breakdown we use with clients, with what works and what does not. HubSpot research puts marketing-team AI adoption at 71%, and the productivity lift is now well-documented.

What does AI do brilliantly in 2026 content workflows?

AI compresses five tasks well: research summarisation, outline generation, variant production at scale, first-pass translation, and metadata authoring (alt text, meta descriptions, schema).

  • Research compression. Twenty competitor articles summarised in five minutes, with claims tagged for verification.
  • Outline generation. Topic plus target keyword plus intent gives a usable structure in seconds. Edit the structure, not the blank page.
  • Variant production. Ten ad headlines, six email subject lines, twelve CTA buttons. The lift over a single creative is real.
  • Translation drafts. First-pass localisation across five EU languages, then native edit.
  • Metadata. Meta descriptions, image alt text, schema markup. The work no one wants to do.

What does AI still fail at?

AI fails at original opinions, first-hand experience stories, voice consistency over long pieces, and original research. The patterns are statistical; the failures are predictable.

Original opinions: AI writes what is common, by definition. Specific personal stories: the detail that makes content stick comes from real life. Voice consistency over long pieces: subtle drift creeps in after 800 words. Original research: AI cannot run a survey, interview a customer, or do regression analysis with judgement.

What is the workflow that produces shippable AI-assisted articles?

Six steps: human brief (15 min), AI research and outline (10 min), human voice pass on intro and conclusion (60 min), AI fill-in on procedural sections (5 min), human edit pass (30 min), AI utility pass for metadata (5 min). About two hours total for 1500 words.

  1. Human brief: topic, angle, target reader, three claims to support.
  2. AI research and outline using ChatGPT, Claude, or Surfer to surface sources and structure.
  3. Human writer drafts introduction, conclusion, and any section needing opinion or story.
  4. AI drafts the procedural sections (the "here are five steps" parts).
  5. Human edit pass: trim, sharpen, add specific examples, fix voice.
  6. AI utility pass: meta description, alt text, FAQ schema.

A skilled human-only writer takes four to six hours for the same output. A pure AI piece takes 20 minutes and reads like a pure AI piece.

How do you keep AI voice out of the published version?

Edit ruthlessly for AI tells: stacked triads, uniform sentence length, the most-overused verbs, and symmetric balanced structures. Specific list below.

Watch for these patterns: stacked triads back-to-back, sentences of identical length, the most-overused AI verbs (use the banned list at Search Engine Land or the project AGENTS.md), and the symmetric construction comparing X with Y. Replace adjectives with numbers.

If you have a content strategy based on volume, it is breaking. If it was based on point of view, AI gives you compounding output. Use the patterns inside the UNIFY Framework to map content to the right buyer state.

Frequently asked questions

Does Google penalise AI-assisted content?

No. Google's policy is about helpful content, not authorship. AI-assisted content that is reviewed, accurate, and useful ranks fine. Pure scaled AI spam gets demoted.

Should I disclose AI assistance?

Disclose when AI did substantial drafting. Skip disclosure when it only assists with research or metadata. Industry practice has settled here.

How many pieces per week can a small team publish?

With this workflow, one mid-sized team ships 5 to 8 well-edited 1500-word pieces a week. Distribution becomes the bottleneck.

Do AI Overviews kill organic traffic?

They reduce informational click-through 30 to 60% on affected queries. Comparison and transactional queries are less affected. Re-balance toward those.

What about agentic content delivery?

MCP servers and llms.txt are early. Ship them as low-cost insurance. Do not rebuild strategy around them yet.

The future of content is humans and AI in the right order. The writer is still the writer. The assistant just got faster.

item.title: Integrating branding with performance marketing for sustainable growth
item.excerpt:encoded: The false choice between brand building and performance marketing is killing long-term growth.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Brand and performance are treated as separate teams with separate budgets. That split costs growth. Ehrenberg-Bass research backs the 60/40 brand-to-performance split as a starting point, not a rule. The integrated model measures brand investments by their effect on performance metrics over time and keeps performance creative on-brand.

The 60/40 brand-to-performance split that the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute popularised is a starting point, not a rule. The real question is whether your brand and performance work are reinforcing each other or running in parallel. Most companies run them in parallel. The cost shows up in CAC over 18 months.

Why does the brand-performance split cost growth?

The split costs growth in three ways: performance creative drifts off-brand, brand investments are measured wrong or not at all, and budget shifts to whatever can be measured this quarter.

  • Performance creative drifts off-brand. The fastest-converting ad copy is often the most generic. Without brand guard-rails, performance teams optimise for tactical wins that erode positioning.
  • Brand work gets measured wrong. Tracking lift in branded search, direct traffic, and aided recall is uncommon. The brand team defaults to creative awards, not commerce.
  • Budgets shift to what can be measured. Performance always wins this argument because the dashboard is real and the brand-lift study is annual.

How do you tell if brand and performance are integrated?

Three signals: branded search volume is on the weekly dashboard, performance teams use the same brand book as brand teams, and marketing-mix modelling is the planning tool instead of last-click.

  1. Branded search volume on the weekly dashboard. If brand spend increases, branded search rises 4 to 12 weeks later. If branded search is flat or falling, your brand investment is not landing.
  2. Performance teams use the brand book. Tone, colour, type, messaging. Performance can produce more variants, but the brand bar holds.
  3. Marketing-mix modelling instead of last-click. MMM credits brand for what it earns: the long tail of conversions that look like direct traffic.

What is the playbook for aligning the two without a reorg?

Five moves: shared OKR on new-customer revenue, weekly brand-lead review of performance creative, brand measured against branded search not awards, 10% quarterly reallocation toward high-trust channels, semi-annual incrementality test on largest paid channel.

Run the moves in order. The shared OKR is the unlock; without it the rest stalls. Reforge's growth content has documented the integration pattern across high-performing teams.

What does success look like in numbers?

A retailer we worked with shifted from 85/15 performance/brand to 55/45 over four quarters. Branded search rose 31%, blended CAC dropped 18%, total revenue grew 22% in 12 months.

The performance team initially resisted the shift because the dashboard they reported on showed only the performance side. Once branded search and direct traffic joined the dashboard, the picture changed and so did the team's incentives. Use the ROI Forecaster to model the shift before committing to it.

Frequently asked questions

Should small companies do brand work?

Yes, but cheaply. Founder-led content, partnerships, and earned media count. The mistake is to treat brand as something only big companies can afford.

How long until brand investments show in performance?

4 to 12 weeks for branded search lift. 6 to 12 months for sustained CAC improvement.

Who owns the integration?

The CMO or the most senior marketer on the team. Without one accountable owner, the split persists.

What about long-term brand metrics?

Aided awareness, unaided awareness, and brand-funnel surveys all matter; run quarterly with a stable methodology. Wynter, Sparktoro, and YouGov panels make this cheaper than it used to be.

How do you justify brand spend to the CFO?

Use the MMM output. The CFO will accept a model. They will not accept "brand is important" without numbers.

The brands that grow most reliably do not pick brand or performance. They run both with the same dashboard. See how we structure this for mid-market clients.

item.title: AI marketing for B2B: opportunities, risks, and real results
item.excerpt:encoded: B2B marketing is ripe for AI transformation, but the stakes are higher.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

AI marketing in B2B is messier than in B2C because the sales cycle is longer and the decision-makers are committees. The biggest wins live in account research, predictive lead scoring, and outbound personalisation. According to Salesforce State of Marketing, 75% of B2B marketers say generative AI has improved campaign performance. The biggest risks are hallucinations in customer-facing material and weak data hygiene.

B2B marketers got a slower start with AI than their B2C peers for a fair reason: more is at stake per touchpoint. A bad ad headline costs a click. A hallucinated stat in an enterprise sales deck costs the deal. Here is where the wins are real and where caution is justified, based on engagements we run at Booming Venture and the published Gartner CMO survey data.

Where does AI move the number for B2B marketing teams?

Four areas: account research summarisation, predictive lead scoring on closed-won data, AI-personalised outbound with intent signals, and AI-drafted content briefs.

  • Account research. Summarise a target company's 10-K, recent press, exec moves, and tech stack in minutes. SDRs go in warmer; AEs send more relevant follow-ups.
  • Predictive lead scoring. Trained on your own closed-won and closed-lost data, it beats hand-built rules by 15 to 30% on SQL-to-closed. Biggest win when you have at least 1,000 closed deals.
  • Outbound personalisation. AI first lines tied to a verified intent signal raise reply rates from 1 to 2% to 4 to 8% in sequences we have run. The signal matters more than the AI.
  • Content briefs and SEO. AI condenses competitive content and identifies content gaps. Brief stays human-edited; writing stays mostly human.

Where are the real risks?

Hallucinated facts in customer-facing material, brand voice drift, dirty CRM data feeding confident wrong predictions, and procurement / EU AI Act compliance questions from enterprise buyers.

  • Hallucinated facts. Stats that do not exist, attributed quotes that were never said. Mitigate with verification workflow and source-grounding.
  • Brand voice drift. Distinctive B2B voices (Drift, Gong, Intercom) lose voice fast if AI output ships raw.
  • Data quality. AI built on dirty CRM data makes confident wrong predictions. Spend half the budget on data hygiene before the model.
  • Procurement and compliance. Enterprise buyers ask about your AI use. Have a one-pager ready. The EU AI Act Article 50 transparency rules apply from August 2026.

What does good look like in practice?

A B2B SaaS company we work with shipped three AI use cases in one quarter: predictive scoring, outbound personalisation, and AI-drafted SDR follow-ups. Pipeline up 41%, SDR meetings per day up from 1.4 to 2.8, in 90 days.

None of the three use cases involved AI-written long-form content. None involved a chatbot. The wins were operational, not flashy.

Where should you not start?

Avoid AI in customer support unless you have a high-trust deflection use case, avoid AI-generated case studies, and avoid AI sales-call summaries going directly to prospects. B2B trust bar is higher than B2C.

Recovery from a bad B2B AI interaction takes months. The blast radius of one bad output reaching procurement is larger than for any consumer brand. Risk-rank your candidate use cases before sequencing.

Frequently asked questions

Do we need a data scientist?

Not for starter wins. Klaviyo, HubSpot AI, Apollo, and Clay all ship usable models. You need one when you train on your own data, year two.

How long before we see results?

Lead scoring: 4 to 6 weeks. Outbound personalisation: 30 days. Account research: time saved immediately, revenue attribution harder.

What does this cost?

Mid-market B2B: $3K to $8K per month in tools plus one senior marketer's time.

How do we handle the EU AI Act?

Limited-risk obligations from August 2026. Disclose AI use in chatbots, mark AI-generated content, keep AI literacy training for staff. Anthropic and OpenAI publish compliance guidance.

Should we build our own LLM?

Almost never. Use foundation models with retrieval over your own data. Fine-tuning is only worth it past 100K+ examples and a clear quality gap.

B2B AI marketing pays back faster than most teams expect, only when the use cases are picked carefully. Start with one workflow, prove the loop, then expand. See where your funnel is leaking before deciding which workflow to attack first.

item.title: Low-hanging growth: what you can improve tomorrow using AI
item.excerpt:encoded: You don’t need a complete overhaul to see AI results.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

If you want AI results inside a month, do not start with a model. Start with three workflow changes: AI-drafted lifecycle emails, predictive subject-line testing, and dynamic product recommendations. Klaviyo benchmarks show personalised recommendations lift email revenue per recipient 15 to 35%. Each ships in four weeks and costs almost nothing to test.

Most companies new to AI try the impressive use cases first: chatbots, content engines, predictive segmentation across the whole CRM. Those projects take six months and often deliver nothing for a year. Here are three that ship in four weeks.

What is the lowest-effort first AI win for most teams?

AI-drafted lifecycle emails are the lowest-effort first win. Most lifecycle programs were written once and never updated; rewriting the worst three emails with AI variants lifts revenue per email 8 to 25%.

Pull the last 12 weeks of performance data for each email in your lifecycle. Identify the bottom three by click-through. Brief AI with the goal of each email, the audience, the tone, and the offer. Ask for three variations. A/B test the best variation against the current version for 14 days. Lock in the winner. Repeat next month with the next worst-performing email. HubSpot State of Marketing data confirms the pattern at scale.

How does predictive subject-line testing change open rates?

Predictive subject-line testing lifts open rates 3 to 8% on average. The feature is already in your ESP (Klaviyo, HubSpot, Customer.io); most teams have not switched it on.

The feature scores subject lines against historical performance from across the platform. It is not perfect, but it eliminates the worst third of bad subject lines automatically. Switch it on for one campaign this week. The setup time is one checkbox.

What about dynamic product recommendations on ecommerce?

Switching static "you might also like" blocks to AI-driven recommenders lifts attached revenue per session 12 to 30%. The bigger your catalogue, the bigger the lift.

Shopify Magic, Klaviyo predictive recommendations, and Algolia all do this out of the box. Shopify reports consistent compounding lift on stores that switch. The work is configuration, not engineering.

What are the honest caveats?

Three: lift compounds only if you maintain the loop, the win comes from the loop not the AI, and always have a control group. Half the teams that report failure never measured the baseline.

  • Maintain the loop. Test losers, lock in winners, then keep testing. Stagnation costs as much as never starting.
  • The win is the loop, not the AI. A poorly run test still loses. Build an experiment calendar, not a one-time hack.
  • Always have a control. Half the failed cases we audit never measured the baseline before launching.

Frequently asked questions

Which of the three should I start with?

Whichever you have the cleanest baseline for. If your lifecycle is a mess, fix it first because the upside is biggest there.

Do I need new tools?

No, in most cases. The features are inside the tools you already pay for. Audit your stack before buying.

What if I have no ecommerce?

B2B equivalents: AI-drafted SDR sequences, predictive demo-show-up reminders, AI-summarised CRM activity for AEs before calls.

How small is too small to bother?

Below 5,000 monthly recipients, predictive features have too little signal. Stay manual until your list scales.

What about AI-driven send-time?

Worth turning on for any list above 10K. Lift 5 to 15% on opens with one checkbox setup.

Pick one. Run it for four weeks. Measure the lift. The point is not the experiment, it is showing your team that AI changes the number when pointed at the right workflow. Our Growth Optimization engagement sequences the next three after the first.

item.title: ROI optimization for Netherlands SME: a data-driven approach
item.excerpt:encoded: Dutch SMEs face unique market challenges.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Dutch SMEs face a specific ROI problem: small home market, EU privacy rules that bite, and a marketing landscape over-indexed on agencies. CBS data puts the Dutch population at 17.9 million; paid channels saturate fast. The wins are usually in the basics: fix the funnel before scaling spend, use first-party data well, commit to two channels.

We work with SMEs across Rotterdam, Amsterdam, Utrecht, and Eindhoven. Dutch SMEs over-spend on paid media and under-invest in the unsexy parts of marketing that compound. Here is what we have learned about ROI optimisation in the Netherlands, with the patterns that recur.

Why do Dutch SMEs leak ROI more than they should?

Three reasons recur: the home market is small and saturates fast, agencies dominate execution and resist mix changes, and EU privacy enforcement bites earlier than most teams plan for.

  • Small home market. 17.9 million people. Paid channels saturate within 12 to 18 months for most B2C brands.
  • Agencies dominate execution. Many SMEs outsource all marketing to one agency. The agency's incentive is to keep doing what they did last quarter.
  • EU privacy rules apply with teeth. The Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens enforces more aggressively than most EU regulators. Tracking, consent, and cookie compliance must be solid before paid scaling makes sense.

Which basics pay back the fastest?

Three: fix the funnel before scaling spend, connect first-party data systems you already pay for, and commit to two channels you can master rather than diluting across six.

  1. Fix the funnel before scaling spend. If your conversion rate is 1.2% against an industry average of 2.5%, the highest-ROI move is fixing checkout, form length, page speed, and trust signals. Use the Funnel Leak Calculator to size the missed revenue.
  2. Use first-party data well. Most Dutch SMEs have email lists they barely use, CRM data they do not segment, and product usage data that never reaches marketing. Connect them.
  3. Commit to two channels. A diluted budget across six channels produces nothing measurable. For B2B SMEs the usual pair is LinkedIn plus high-intent Google search. For B2C it depends on category.

What does not work for Dutch SMEs?

Three patterns fail: trying to scale Meta forever in a 12M-user market, translated US blog content that does not rank in NL SERPs, and outsourcing strategy to the agency that also runs ads.

The Netherlands has fewer than 12 million Facebook users. Saturation is fast. Translated US blog posts do not rank in Dutch SERPs; original Dutch content with Dutch examples does. And outsourcing strategy to the agency that also runs ads is a conflict of interest. Keep strategy in-house, outsource execution.

What does a real Dutch SME case look like?

A Rotterdam B2B services client doubled revenue on the same €40K monthly spend in 12 months. Three changes: consolidated to LinkedIn plus Google, set up HubSpot to Looker Studio reporting, redesigned the demo booking funnel.

The funnel work alone added an estimated €420K in annual revenue. The agency that ran the original six-channel split is still doing fine for other clients; that mix simply did not work for this SME.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to be on Meta?

Only if your buyer is. For most Dutch B2B and high-consideration B2C, the answer is no, or only for retargeting.

Is Dutch-language content worth it?

Yes for local-intent and SME audiences. English works fine for global B2B and tech.

How much should I spend on marketing?

Healthy benchmarks: 6 to 10% of revenue for B2B SMEs, 10 to 15% for B2C, more during growth phases.

What about EU AI Act compliance?

Limited-risk use cases need disclosure. Chatbots, AI-generated content, profiling features. Have a one-paragraph disclosure ready.

Should I use Dutch agencies or specialists?

Specialists per discipline beat one generalist agency in most cases. Specialists are cheaper to fire if they underperform.

ROI optimisation is rarely about a better channel. It is about fewer channels, run with more rigour, against a cleaner funnel. Our engagements always start with the funnel audit.

item.title: Marketing funnel: how it works in 2025
item.excerpt:encoded: The traditional marketing funnel is dead.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

The linear marketing funnel was already wrong in 2018. In 2025 it is a useful illustration and a poor operating model. Gartner B2B Buyer research shows buyers complete 60 to 80% of evaluation before contacting sales. The functional replacement is a state-based model with three buyer states: not in market, in market researching, in market deciding.

Awareness, interest, desire, action. The triangle E. St. Elmo Lewis drew in 1898 still gets reprinted in textbooks. It worked because the salesperson controlled information flow. It breaks now because the buyer does. Modern buyers move sideways, skip stages, and reverse direction inside a single research session.

What changed between 2018 and 2025?

Four changes broke the linear funnel: information became infinite, trust collapsed away from brands, B2B buying committees grew to 6 to 11 stakeholders, and the same buyer now touches 6+ channels in one session.

  1. Information is infinite. Buyers can answer any question themselves. Awareness is no longer a marketer's gift to bestow.
  2. Trust collapsed. Buyers trust peers, reviews, unaffiliated sources. They distrust ads, sales reps, and content from the brand itself.
  3. Buying committees grew. The average B2B SaaS purchase involves 6 to 11 stakeholders (Gartner).
  4. Channels multiplied. One buyer touches LinkedIn, Twitter, a podcast, Reddit, G2, and Google in a single research session.

What replaces the funnel as an operating model?

Three buyer states replace the funnel: not in market (95% of any audience at any moment), in market researching, in market deciding. Each state has different goals, channels, and metrics.

State 1: Not in market

Goal: be top of mind when a project starts. Tools: brand investment, thought leadership, podcasts, PR. Metric: branded search, direct traffic, aided recall. The Ehrenberg-Bass 95-5 rule applies here: 95% of any target audience is in this state at any moment.

State 2: In market, researching

Goal: be on the shortlist. Tools: comparison content, case studies, customer reviews on G2 or Capterra, ungated technical resources. Metric: traffic to comparison pages, demo requests, shortlist appearances.

State 3: In market, deciding

Goal: easy to say yes. Tools: high-trust signals (security pages, customer logos, named references), short demos, transparent pricing, fast follow-up from sales. Metric: shortlist-to-close rate.

How do you actually use this model?

Map every current marketing activity to one of the three states, reallocate 10% per quarter toward state 1 until you hit ~30/40/30, and measure each state with its fit-for-purpose metric.

  1. Map current marketing to the three states. Most teams discover 80% of budget is in state 3, where the smallest gains live.
  2. Reallocate 10% per quarter toward state 1 until you hit roughly 30/40/30.
  3. Measure each state with the metric that fits, not last-click revenue across the board.

Use the ROI Forecaster to model the reallocation before you commit.

Frequently asked questions

Is the funnel useful for anything?

Yes, for budget conversations with finance. They like triangles. Just do not run the team off it.

How do I measure state 1?

Branded search in Google Search Console, direct traffic in GA4, quarterly aided-awareness survey.

What about middle of the funnel?

It shrinks every year as buyers compress evaluation. Spend less on nurture, more on signal capture.

Does this work for ecommerce?

Yes, with different mechanics. The three states map to: hasn't bought yet, browsing now, in cart. The principle holds.

How do I get sales aligned with this?

Share the dashboard. Sales naturally prefers state 3 leads; show them state 2 leads have higher LTV when nurtured right.

Stop running the funnel. Start running three programs for three buyer states. The UNIFY Framework implements this structure across the marketing stack.

item.title: The hidden costs of inefficient marketing funnels
item.excerpt:encoded: Funnel inefficiencies don’t just reduce conversions, they compound into massive hidden costs.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Funnel inefficiencies cost more than the dashboard shows. The visible cost is lower revenue; the hidden costs are CAC inflation, exhausted teams, wasted ad spend, lost talent, and slower compounding. Total: 2 to 4x the visible loss. Klaviyo benchmarks confirm the multiplier across B2C; B2B is closer to 3 to 5x.

Every funnel has leaks. Most teams know roughly where. Few teams know what those leaks actually cost. Here is the math behind the hidden costs, and how to size them for your own business.

What is the visible cost of a funnel leak?

The visible cost is the direct revenue gap between your current conversion rate and benchmark. 10,000 visitors at 2% versus 3% with €500 AOV = €50K/month visible. The hidden costs multiply that by 2 to 4x.

Take 10,000 monthly visitors, a 2% conversion rate, and a €500 average order value. Monthly revenue: €100K. Fix the funnel to 3% conversion: €150K. That is the obvious €50K per month. The hidden costs are bigger.

What hidden costs do teams ignore?

Five hidden costs: CAC inflation from bidding against yourself for more traffic, sales-team thrash on bad leads, lost compounding from referrals and word-of-mouth, talent attrition, and slower decision-making in noisy dashboards.

  • CAC inflation. A leaky funnel pulls in more traffic to hit the same revenue. More traffic means higher CPM and CPC because you bid against yourself. 30% conversion gap typically means 20 to 40% higher blended CAC.
  • Sales team thrash. Bad leads reach sales. SDRs spend hours on prospects who were never going to buy. AEs hold demos that go nowhere. 25 to 40% of productive capacity goes to funnel inefficiency.
  • Compounding loss. Every lost conversion is also a lost referral, lost word-of-mouth, lost LTV. Adds another 1.5 to 2x the direct revenue loss over 12 months for businesses with normal retention.
  • Talent attrition. Marketing and sales teams watching effort disappear into a broken funnel burn out. Glassdoor-visible cost: turnover. Hidden cost: institutional knowledge.
  • Slower decision-making. Leaky funnels make every dashboard noisy. Teams spend meetings arguing about what numbers mean. Six months pass.

What does the worked example look like end to end?

A SaaS account we audited had 1.4% demo-request rate against benchmark 2.8%. Visible cost €120K/month MRR. All-in including hidden costs: €3.2M annual loss against a €60K fix budget.

Visible cost: €120K/month in lost MRR (€1.44M annually). Hidden: CAC inflation €40K/month, sales productivity loss €30K/month, compounding effect €1M annual. Total annual cost: €3.2M. Cost to fix: €60K of consulting plus six weeks of in-house work. The ratio is typical, not exceptional.

How do you find your own hidden costs?

Three steps: calculate conversion rate at each stage against benchmark, apply the visible-cost formula, then multiply by 2 to estimate all-in. That number is the budget you can justify for the fix.

  1. Calculate conversion rate at each funnel stage. Compare against benchmarks (Klaviyo, Search Engine Land publish category data). Identify the worst gap.
  2. Apply the visible cost formula. Use the Funnel Leak Calculator for the math.
  3. Multiply by 2 to estimate all-in cost. That is the budget you can justify spending on the fix.

Frequently asked questions

How much should I spend to fix a funnel leak?

Up to half the all-in annual cost. Most teams underinvest because they only see the visible cost.

What about A/B test losses?

Properly run tests are an investment, not a cost. The losses tell you what does not work. The wins compound.

Which stage usually has the biggest leak?

For B2B SaaS: demo-to-close. For ecommerce: checkout. For high-consideration B2C: form-to-lead.

How fast do fixes pay back?

Mobile checkout fixes: 30 days. Form-length reduction: 14 days. Pricing-page rewrite: 30 to 60 days.

Should I hire a CRO consultant?

Worth it once your annual digital revenue exceeds €1M. Below that, the in-house team plus a checklist (see our CRO audit post) is enough.

The dashboard shows the visible cost. The hidden cost is usually 2 to 4x. Add it up before you decide what a fix is worth.

item.title: Customer retention AI strategies for 2025
item.excerpt:encoded: Acquiring customers is expensive; retaining them is profitable.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Acquisition is expensive, retention is profitable. Harvard Business Review research shows a 5% retention lift can raise profits 25 to 95% depending on category. AI changes retention by spotting churn signals before humans, personalising lifecycle at scale, and predicting which customers to invest in. Three plays pay back fastest.

Most marketing leaders overspend on acquisition by a factor of two to four. Retention math is simple but unsexy: a 5% retention lift is worth more than a 25% acquisition lift in most categories and costs less to achieve. AI makes the retention work faster.

What is predictive churn scoring and how does it work?

Predictive churn scoring is a model trained on historical churn that flags at-risk accounts 30 to 60 days before they would churn. Modern tools (Gainsight, Catalyst, HubSpot health score) ship usable models out of the box.

Train on declining product usage, late payments, support tickets with negative sentiment, fewer logins from key users. The lift comes from the intervention, not the prediction. Save 30% of flagged accounts and you have moved the number meaningfully.

How does AI-driven lifecycle personalisation lift retention?

Behaviour-driven lifecycle sends different emails to different customers based on what they did. Klaviyo and Customer.io ship behaviour-driven flows that lift revenue per recipient 15 to 35%.

Static lifecycle programs send the same email on day 7 to every customer. AI-driven lifecycle reads the customer's actual behaviour. The customer who set up the product gets advanced tips. The customer who has not logged in gets onboarding help. Klaviyo benchmarks document the lift across categories.

What is AI-driven win-back and why does it triple reactivation?

AI-driven win-back tags lost customers by churn reason (price, fit, competitor switch, neglect) and sends segment-specific messages instead of batch-blast discounts. Reactivation rates triple in our work.

Building this takes work: tag lost customers with churn reason, design segment-specific sequences, route responses to the right owner. Three months from start to first results.

Where does AI retention fail?

AI retention fails in three places: replacing human relationships for top-tier accounts, predicting churn with under 18 months of history, and B2B retention strategies that ignore product fit.

  • Replacing human relationships for top-tier accounts. C-suite calls and dinners still matter.
  • Predicting churn with less than 18 months of history. The model has nothing to learn from.
  • B2B retention that ignores product fit. AI cannot fix a customer who never should have signed.

What should you measure?

Four metrics: gross revenue retention (CFO-friendly), net revenue retention by cohort, lift from each intervention against a hold-out control, and cost per retained customer versus cost per acquired.

  1. Gross revenue retention (the boring one, the one CFOs care about).
  2. Net revenue retention by cohort, not aggregated.
  3. Lift from each AI intervention measured against a hold-out control.
  4. Cost per retained customer compared to cost per acquired customer.

Frequently asked questions

Where should I start?

Predictive churn scoring if you have at least 12 months of churn history. Lifecycle personalisation if you do not.

How much does this cost?

Mid-market: $2K to $8K per month in tools plus one senior owner's quarter time. Enterprise: $30K to $150K per year for Gainsight-class platforms.

Will it work for B2C?

Yes, with different mechanics. Klaviyo and Bloomreach handle B2C retention well.

What about CSAT and NPS?

Lagging indicators. Useful for direction, not for daily decisions. Pair with in-product behaviour signals.

Is this GDPR safe?

Yes if you process under contract performance or legitimate interest, document the balancing test, and offer opt-out per GDPR Art. 21.

Retention is the largest unfixed problem in most marketing programs. AI lowers the cost of fixing it. Start with churn prediction, then lifecycle, then win-back.

item.title: 5 marketing automation mistakes that are losing you customers
item.excerpt:encoded: Marketing automation should nurture relationships, not damage them.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Marketing automation is supposed to scale relationships, not punish them. The five mistakes that turn subscribers into unsubscribes: over-sending, generic personalisation, broken context awareness, rigid time-based sequences, and no handoff from automation to humans. Brevo industry data puts the unsubscribe tipping point at around 4 to 6 sends per week per subscriber.

Marketing automation platforms were sold to teams as a way to scale 1:1 communication. In practice they often scale 1:millions, badly. The five mistakes below turn subscribers into unsubscribes faster than anything else.

Why does over-sending wreck deliverability and trust?

Above 4 to 6 emails per week per subscriber, list health collapses. Open rates fall, unsubscribes spike, spam complaints rise, and inboxes start filtering future sends from the same domain.

Every team thinks one more email cannot hurt. Every team is wrong. The breaking point varies by industry but the pattern is consistent. Fix: cap weekly sends per subscriber. Use frequency suppression rules. If a customer received three campaigns in the last seven days, do not send a fourth.

What is wrong with generic personalisation?

Hi [First Name] is not personalisation; neither is dynamic content blocks that rotate generic options. Real personalisation sends different emails to different people based on what they did.

Segment by behaviour. Last purchase category, recent product views, lifecycle stage, NPS score, time since last purchase. Send each segment a different message, not the same message with a different name token. Klaviyo benchmarks show behavioural segments outperform demographic segments 3 to 5x on revenue per recipient.

How does broken context awareness kill retention?

Automation that ignores negative signals creates absurd interactions: surveys to angry customers, renewal reminders to churned ones, promo offers mid-complaint. Connect support, billing, and sales systems to pause triggers.

The customer just opened a support ticket. The automation sends them a survey asking how happy they are. The customer just churned. The automation sends them a renewal reminder. Fix: pause automation triggers based on negative signals. The cost is integration work, the saving is a lot of angry replies.

Why are rigid time-based sequences a problem?

Time-based sequences ignore behaviour. The customer who used the product for two weeks gets the same day-7 email as the customer who has not logged in once. Switch to behaviour-driven branches.

Many lifecycle programs are time-based and never updated. Day 1 welcome, day 3 product tour, day 7 case study, day 14 promo. The sequence ignores what the customer actually did. Behaviour-driven branches send the day-7 email only if they completed the day-3 tutorial. Send the renewal reminder only if usage is healthy.

What is the human handoff that automation drops?

Automation usually drops the conversation at exactly the moment a human should pick it up. The high-value customer replied to an automated email; the AE never sees it. Route replies.

When a high-value customer replies to any automated email, surface it to the account manager that day. The investment is minimal, the retention impact is measurable. Set up a Zapier or workflow that creates a CRM task on every reply.

Frequently asked questions

How many emails per week is too many?

Depends on category and engagement. Most B2C ecommerce: 3 to 5 weekly per active subscriber. B2B newsletters: 1 weekly. Watch unsubscribe-per-send over 0.5% as a warning.

How do I test if my automation is broken?

Subscribe to your own automation under a fake account that mimics a real customer. Live in it for 30 days. The bad sequences will be obvious.

Should I scrap my automation and start over?

Rarely. Audit the five points above and fix the worst first. A rebuild costs more than the incremental fixes earn.

What about SMS frequency?

Lower cap. 1 to 2 weekly maximum for most categories. SMS unsubscribe risk is higher than email.

Is AI making this worse?

Only if you point it at the wrong workflow. AI inside a behaviour-driven program is great; AI inside a static one accelerates the damage.

Marketing automation is a force multiplier. It multiplies whatever you point at it. Point it at segmented, behaviour-driven, context-aware communication and it multiplies retention. Our Growth Optimization engagement rebuilds the four common failures above.

item.title: Social media ROI measurement: beyond vanity metrics
item.excerpt:encoded: Likes and follows don’t pay the bills.
item.content:encoded:
Key takeaways

Measuring social ROI is hard because most teams measure the wrong things. Vanity metrics tell you nothing about revenue. SparkToro analysis puts organic-social reach decay at 60 to 80% on most platforms since 2020. The metrics that matter: share of voice, engagement quality from named target accounts, conversion-attributed revenue, and influence on direct traffic / branded search.

Every CMO eventually asks: what is social earning us? The answer most agencies give is wrong because they measure what the platform reports, not what the business cares about.

Which metrics should you stop reporting?

Stop reporting followers, likes, reach, and impressions as primary metrics. They were once useful proxies for awareness; algorithms now decide what gets shown, so the proxies broke.

You can have 100K followers and reach 2% of them. Reporting reach without context is dashboard theatre. Replace with the four metrics below.

Which four metrics actually measure social ROI?
